translations.text: You have often heard about the Saviour's resurrection, how on this day he arose from death; but we wish to remind you, so that it does not slip from your memory.
"When Christ had been buried, the Jews said to their governor Pilate, 'Lo, sir, the deceiver who has been slain here,
[?] said frequently, when he was alive, that he would arise from death on the third day:" and so on.
We now say: if anyone had stolen his body, he would not have unclothed it, because theft loves no delay.
On that same day Christ appeared to Peter and to two others of his disciples, and comforted them.
"Then at last the Saviour came to his disciples, where they were gathered, and said to them, Peace be among you; it is I, do not be afraid.
Then they were frightened, and thought that it was some spirit. Then he said to them, 'Why are you frightened, and why do you think such different things about me?
Look at my hands and my feet, which were pierced through with nails. Touch me and see: if I were a spirit, I would not have flesh and bone," and so on.
The Saviour then frequently appeared to his disciples, and directed them in the teaching and in the faith, how they should teach all mankind;
and on the fortieth day after his resurrection he ascended bodily to heaven, to his Father.
But we have now told you a much greater part of the sequence of Christ's book than this day's gospel contains, for the strengthening of your faith.
Now we will set out for you the exposition of this day's gospel, following the exposition of the holy Pope Gregory.
My dearest brothers, you have heard that the holy women who followed the Lord in his life came to his tomb with the precious ointment,
and him whom they had loved in life they wished to serve, when dead, with human devotion. But this deed signifies something to be done in God's Church.
We who believe in Christ's resurrection truly come to his tomb with precious ointment if we are filled with the fragrance of holy virtues, and if we seek our Lord with the good report of good works.
The women who brought the ointment saw angels; because those see the heavenly angels who, with the fragrances of good works, long for the journey on high.
The angel rolled the lid off the tomb. He did not do this to make room for Christ to go out, but to show people that he had risen.

He who came as a mortal into this world, born through the closed womb of the virgin, was without doubt the same one who, when he arose immortal, could go out of the world from the tomb while it was still shut.
The angel sat on the right side of the tomb. The right hand signifies eternal life, and the left hand this present life.
The angel rightly sat on the right hand, because he made known that the Saviour had then passed beyond the corruptions of this present life, and was then abiding, immortal, in eternal things.
The messenger was clothed in a shining garment, because he proclaimed the joy of this festival, and our glory.
Shall we say it was our festival or the angels'? We say truly that it was both ours and theirs.
The Saviour's resurrection is our festival and joy, because by his resurrection he led us to the immortality for which we were created.
His resurrection was the joy of the angels, because God fills up their number when he brings us to heaven.
The angel encouraged the women, saying thus, "Do not be afraid": as if he had said, Let those be afraid who do not love the coming of angels;
let those be terrified who are oppressed by fleshly lusts and have no hope of the company of angels. Why are you afraid, you who see your companions?
"His appearance was like lightning, and his raiment as white as snow." Truly in lightning there is terror, and in snow the gentleness of brightness.
Rightly was the herald of Christ's resurrection so formed; because when he himself comes to the great judgment, he will be very terrible to the sinful, and very gentle to the righteous.
He said, "You seek the Saviour: he has risen: he is not here." He was not then bodily in the tomb, he who is everywhere through his divine might.
There lay behind the garment in which he had been wrapped, because he did not care for the earthly garment after he had risen from death.
Though a dead man is wrapped in a garment, the garment does not rise again with the man any the sooner. Instead he is clothed with the heavenly garment after his resurrection.
It is well said of the Saviour that he would go before his companions into Galilee. 'Galilee' means 'passing over.'
The Saviour had then passed from suffering to resurrection, from death to life, from torment to glory.
And if we pass from sins to holy virtues, then we may see the Saviour after our journey out of this life.
Truly there are two lives: the one we know; the other was unknown to us before Christ's coming. The one life is mortal, the other immortal.
But the Saviour came and took on the one life, and revealed the other. The one life he showed by his death, and the other by his resurrection.
If he had promised us mortal men resurrection and eternal life, and yet would not show it through himself, who then would have believed his promises?
But when he chose to be a man, he also humbled himself to death of his own will, and he rose from death through his divine might, and showed through himself what he had promised us.
Now someone says in his thoughts, 'He could easily rise from death, because he is God: death could not hold him captive.'
Let the man who thinks this hear the answer to his thought. Christ died alone at that time, but he did not rise from death alone; he rose with a great company.
The evangelist Matthew wrote in the book of Christ that many holy people who had died under the old law arose with Christ;
and various wise teachers have said that these people have achieved their resurrection to eternal life, as we all shall do at the end of this world.
The teachers said that the men who were raised would not truly have been witnesses of Christ's resurrection if they had not been raised forever.
Now all unbelief is put out, so that no one should despair of his own resurrection, since the evangelist wrote that many rose with Christ who were mere men, though Christ is God.
Now Gregory the commentator said that it came to his mind how the Jews cried out about Christ when he was fastened on the cross.
They said, "If he is the king of Israel, then let him come down now from the cross, and we will believe in him."

If he had then come down from the cross and would not bear their mockery, then without doubt he would have given us no example of his patience. But he waited a little while, and bore their mockery, and was patient.
But he who would not break away from the cross arose from the tomb. It was a greater wonder that he arose from death than if he had broken away from the cross alive.
It was a greater power that he broke death by his resurrection than if he had saved his life by coming down from the cross.
But when they saw that he did not come down from the cross because of their mockery, but awaited death on it, they believed that he had been overcome and his name blotted out:
but it happened that from that death his name spread throughout all the world. Then their joy was turned into the greatest grief, because their sorrow will be endless.
These things were foreshadowed by the strong Samson, who was in a feud with the people called the Philistines.
Then it happened that he came to their city, which was called Gaza. The Philistines were very glad and besieged the city.
But the strong Samson arose at midnight, seized the city gates, and carried them up onto a hill, to put his enemies to shame.
The strong Samson stood for Christ, the city of Gaza stood for hell, and the Philistines stood for the Jewish people, who set a guard around Christ's tomb.
But Samson would not leave the city empty-handed; he carried the gates up to the hill;
because our Saviour Christ broke the gates of hell and rescued Adam and Eve and his chosen ones of their race. He freely arose from death, and they arose together with him, and he ascended to heaven.
He left the wicked behind to the eternal torments. And now the gate of hell is locked to righteous men, and always open to the unrighteous.
The Jewish people were wretched in being so unbelieving. All creatures recognized their Creator except the Jews alone.
The heavens recognized Christ's birth, for when he was born a new star was seen.
The sea recognized Christ when he walked with dry feet on its waves. The earth recognized him when it all quaked at Christ's resurrection.
The sun recognized him when it was darkened at Christ's passion from midday until the ninth hour. The stones recognized him when they split apart at their Creator's death.
Hell recognized Christ when it let its captives go out because of the Savior's harrowing.
And yet, despite all these signs, the hard-hearted Jews would not turn in faith to the merciful Savior, who wants to help all people who believe in him.

But let us believe that God the Father always was, without beginning, and that the Son was always begotten of the Father, because he is the Wisdom and Might through which the Father created all creatures;
and they were all given life through the Holy Spirit, who is the Will and Love of the Father and of the Son;
these three are one indivisible God, abiding in one Godhead, all of them equally mighty; for whatever is lesser and less mighty is not God.
But the Father sent the Son for our redemption, and he alone took on human nature, and suffered death of his own will, and arose from death on this day,
and ascended to heaven on the fortieth day after his resurrection, before the sight of many people, and reigns with the Almighty Father and the Holy Spirit, now and ever in eternity. Amen.
